How I work

End to end
  1. 00Understand

    Audit what exists, talk to the people who use it, and map who needs what.

    Me, mid-stepasking "but why?" a few too many times
  2. 01Define

    Turn the mess into a model: states, flows, open questions and principles.

    Me, mid-stepcovering walls with boxes and arrows
  3. 02Design

    Flows, wireframes and UI, tested against real constraints and real roles.

    Me, mid-stepmaking ten versions, keeping the simplest
  4. 03Prototype

    Build it for real, often in code with AI, so ideas survive the handoff.

    Me, mid-stepopening a code editor, happily
  5. 04Ship & scale

    Systems, docs and training so the work keeps paying off after launch.

    Me, mid-stepwriting the docs nobody else wants to

A noteThis is the process that has worked best for me so far, not a fixed recipe. Every project bends it a little, so I adapt the steps to suit the problem, the team and the timeline.

00 · ATI Robotics

AtiFLOW

Turning a product rebuilt for every customer into one that any factory can configure.

Role
Product designer, leading product and UX
Platforms
Android tablet, web admin
Scope
V1 audit, V2 and V3 shipped, V4 concept
Read the full case study ↗

Problem

AtiFLOW sits between the people who need material on a factory floor and the robots that deliver it. Every plant sent its data in a different shape, so each new customer meant custom engineering.

Approach

I audited V1 and mapped every flow in the PRD, which surfaced five open questions. A four-level parent and child material model replaced one flat list. Requesters, approvers and admins now share one layout, so a single training session covers every role.

Beyond the handoff

I built the V3 admin as a working React, TypeScript and MUI app in the engineering team's own stack, using Figma MCP and AI to cover edge cases. atiflowadmin.netlify.app ↗ PA01 / 1234

4 plantsLive at Yokohama, rolling out to Amazon, Bekaert and Inoxpa
0 custom buildsA new site is configured, not engineered
4 stepsTo request material, with no typing on the floor

01 · ATI Robotics

Sherpa HMI

A robot panel that a worker, a supervisor and an engineer can each read from where they stand.

Role
UX designer: flows, UI, handoff
Hardware
Kinco panel, 1024 × 600
Tools
FigJam, Figma, Kinco DTools
Read the full case study ↗

Problem

The touch panel on ATI's self-driving robots had grown one screen at a time. Flows took too many steps, and red meant everything from a station name to an emergency stop.

Approach

I mapped every robot state before drawing a screen, then reduced each screen to a status bar, one illustration, one line of text and one action. Colour was given strict meanings: red for danger, green for done, yellow for the robot itself. The design was rebuilt inside DTools, an industrial tool with very little room for design.

12 statesMapped up front: 8 trip steps and 4 interrupts
5 → 2Sub-states an operator has to keep track of
4 robotsShare one framework; only the illustration and a few words change

02 · HP Inc

Echo

A control panel design system for screens from 2.2 to 24 inches.

Role
Interaction designer, design systems team
Users
Product designers and firmware developers
Scope
Library, templates, documentation, training
Read the full case study ↗

Problem

HP designed its control panels in Axure, with visual specs kept in separate documents that sometimes contradicted each other. Firmware developers read tables to work out which components a screen used, and every new screen size meant designing again.

Approach

We moved the team from Axure to Figma and built Echo as a workflow UI library with templates that resize across panel sizes. Each component links to its "how to use" notes, and recorded training sessions helped designers and firmware teams switch tools without a drop in output.

3 librariesGlobal elements, assets and the design system itself
1 switchBetween light and dark themes
Rem-basedSizing with no dependency on Token Studio

03 · Self-initiated · 2024

Travel Quest

Building the brand first, so the product had something to belong to.

Role
Solo: brand, research, dashboard
Tools
Illustrator, Photoshop, Figma
Read the full case study ↗

Brief

A travel platform is launching Experiences, where travellers discover and list activities in the places they visit. Its teams need an internal tool to manage, review and improve those listings.

Approach

I started with the company. From the brand values of authenticity, adventure, connection and community, I sketched a mark that joins a map pin with the letter Q, then set the palette and tested the identity on signage and merchandise. The dashboard design grew from that identity.
